meta.blurb: Charles Darwin pressed his face to the glass beside a puff adder to test himself. The snake struck, and he jumped back anyway. His 1872 book uses faces, animals and babies to show that feelings carry marks of a long past.
meta.bible: Charles Darwin: the English naturalist who wrote the book, published in 1872; patient, curious, careful and modest. Descent of Man: his earlier book of 1871 about the origin of humans. Duchenne: Guillaume-Benjamin Duchenne, a French doctor who used small electric currents to move the muscles of a living face and photographed the results. Rejlander: Oscar Rejlander, a photographer in London whose photographs Darwin used. Zoological Gardens: the zoo in London where Darwin watched monkeys and snakes. Puff adder: a snake at the zoo that Darwin tested himself against. Three principles: Habit (useful actions that become habits), Antithesis (opposite feelings give opposite movements), Nerves (the nervous system acts by itself). Other terms: Expression, Emotion, Blushing, Grief muscles, Shrug, Goosebumps, Questions (a list of questions Darwin sent to people living in other countries). The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals: the title of the book. England, London, Down: Darwin's home village in Kent. Voice and tone: a patient guide who watches closely, tells what Darwin saw and thought, and says plainly where modern scientists now disagree with him. No gore.

B1B2: In 1872 Charles Darwin published a book that asked an unusual question about people and animals. Why do our faces and bodies show what we feel, even when we would prefer to hide it?
Darwin had already argued that humans and other animals share the same ancestors. This book was meant to show that even our feelings carry signs of that long history.
Long before the book, Darwin had kept notes on his own baby son. He watched every smile, frown and cry, and wrote it all down.

Darwin did not only watch people, because animals cannot easily pretend to feel something. He studied the family dog and the horses at home, and he visited the monkeys at the Zoological Gardens in London.
Darwin wanted to know whether people everywhere show feelings in the same way. So he wrote a list of questions and sent it to friends and travellers in many countries.
Drawings can be wrong, and faces move too fast to draw. So Darwin used photographs, which was a very new idea for a science book.
A French doctor named Duchenne used weak electric currents to make the muscles of a face move. His photographs showed Darwin exactly which muscles make which expression.
Darwin's first idea is that useful actions can become habits. A dog turns round and round on a soft rug before lying down, as its wild family once did to flatten the grass.
When you try hard to remember something, you may lift your eyebrows without knowing it. Darwin thought this began as a way to open the eyes wider and see better.
Darwin's second idea is called antithesis, which means that opposite feelings cause opposite movements. A dog that is ready to fight stands tall, with its fur raised and its tail stiff.
A friendly dog does the exact opposite of an angry one. It lowers its body, lays its ears back, and wags its tail from side to side.
Cats show the same pattern of opposites, just as dogs do. A cat ready to fight crouches low with its ears back, but a happy cat stands tall and rubs against a person's legs.
Darwin's third idea is that the nervous system sometimes acts by itself. When a strong feeling arrives, the body can shake or sweat before the person decides anything.
When someone is very afraid, the heart beats hard and the skin turns pale and damp. Darwin noted that the mouth becomes dry, and that the voice can shake or fail.
When an animal is frightened or angry, its fur often stands on end and makes it look larger. Darwin suggested that our own goosebumps may be a small leftover of this old habit.
The voice is also a way to show feelings. Dogs growl, cats purr, and a frightened child screams, and Darwin thought that many of these sounds are very old.
Darwin watched young chimpanzees at the zoo and noticed that when they were tickled, they made a sound like laughter. This suggested to him that laughing is much older than humans.
Many animals move their ears to show their feelings. An angry horse presses its ears flat against its head and may show its teeth before it bites.
When a person sneers, one side of the lip rises and a tooth may show. Darwin thought this was a remnant of the way our distant ancestors bared their teeth.
At the zoo Darwin saw young chimpanzees push out their lips in a long pout when they were disappointed or sulky. He noted that children often do exactly the same.
When a baby screams, it shuts its eyes very tightly. Darwin thought this might protect the eyes from the pressure of blood, although many scientists doubt his explanation today.
Grown people also weep when they feel great sadness. Darwin thought that tears come from the same habits as a baby's screaming, which we keep when we are older.
In sorrow and worry, the inner ends of the eyebrows rise and the corners of the mouth turn down. Darwin found this pattern in many photographs and in many people.
Darwin called the small muscles above the eyes the grief muscles. He noticed that people find it hard to move them on purpose, yet they work by themselves when someone is sad.
In deep despair, a person may sit still with a hanging head and slow movements. Darwin said the whole body loses its energy and seems to sink.
Joy makes the body want to move in all sorts of ways. Children jump and clap, grown-ups laugh and dance, and a dog may leap about for no reason except that it is happy.
In a good laugh, the mouth opens wide and the muscles around the eyes tighten. Darwin noted that people sometimes laugh until tears run down their cheeks.
Love and tenderness have their own quiet expressions, too. A mother's soft smile, her gentle touch and her calm voice all tell her baby that it is safe.
A frown appears when we think hard or when something is difficult. Darwin said the frown narrows the eyes, which shuts out some light and helps us to concentrate.
A sulky child often pushes out the lips and frowns. Darwin said that this look is easy to recognise in children all over the world.
When a person is very determined, the mouth closes firmly and the jaw sets. Darwin thought this firm mouth showed that the person had made up his or her mind.
When someone is angry, the heart beats faster and the face may turn red. The nostrils open wide, the teeth clench, and the hands tighten into fists.
Strong hatred and rage show in a fixed stare and in a body that leans forward. Darwin said that even a person who tries to stay calm may show these signs.
When people feel contempt or scorn, they often turn their heads away and raise the nose slightly. Darwin said this means that they want nothing to do with the person or the thing.
Disgust makes us wrinkle the nose and push out the lower lip, as if to reject bad food. Darwin said that babies show this look from the first weeks of life.
A person who feels guilty often looks down or away and cannot meet your eyes. A proud person does the opposite, holding the head high and looking straight at others.
A shrug means that we do not know or cannot help. We raise the shoulders, turn the palms up and often lift the eyebrows too, and Darwin found this in many countries.
In many places people nod for yes and shake the head for no, and Darwin asked whether this is natural. He found that the signs are common but not used everywhere, so some of them must be learned.
When we are surprised, the eyebrows lift and the eyes and mouth open wide. Darwin thought this opens the eyes to take in as much as possible of what is new.
Fear opens the eyes wide, drains the colour from the face and makes the heart beat hard. Darwin said that in terror a person may freeze, scream or run.
At the zoo Darwin pressed his face to the thick glass of a puff adder's cage. He told himself firmly that he was safe and would not move.
When the snake struck at the glass, Darwin jumped backwards in spite of his promise to himself. His reason knew he was safe, but his body did not listen.
In terror and horror, a person may scream, shake all over, or try to run away. Darwin noted that the body acts before the person has time to think.
Shyness and shame make people lower their eyes and look away. Darwin thought this comes from thinking too much about what others see when they look at us.
Darwin called blushing the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. He knew of no animal that blushes out of shame.
Darwin believed that we blush when we think about what other people think of us. The tiny blood vessels of the face open wider, and the cheeks turn red.
The answers to Darwin's questions came from many parts of the world. They showed that many expressions, such as blushing, frowning and shrugging, were much the same everywhere.
Darwin concluded that most basic expressions are inherited and not invented. They show, he said, that humans are linked with other animals by a long family history.

Scientists still study faces today, and they do not all agree with Darwin. Some find that certain expressions are understood almost everywhere, while others say that culture matters more than he thought.

Darwin ended his book by saying that the study of expression shows how closely we are linked, to each other and to the animals. A face is a window, and everyone can read at least a little of what it says.
C1C2: In 1872, a year after his theory of human descent had set the whole world arguing, Charles Darwin published a book about something far more intimate than fossils or finches. It asked why the face of a person, or of a dog or a monkey, should change so quickly and so visibly whenever a strong feeling passes through the mind. The book was called The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, and it became one of the first great studies of feeling.

The book began as a small part of his earlier work on the descent of man, where Darwin had argued that humans and the other animals share a common ancestry. If that were true, he reasoned, then the way we show anger, fear and joy ought to carry faint echoes of the animals before us. A frown or a snarl might be a kind of living fossil, written on the face instead of in rock.

Years before he wrote the book, Darwin had begun to keep notes on the faces of his own babies, watching how a smile or a scowl first appeared and what seemed to cause it. Babies, he reasoned, have not yet learned to hide anything, and so their faces tell the plainest truth about what lies underneath. He valued those early notes enough to return to them again and again as he wrote.

Darwin was never content to watch only people, for his whole argument depended on comparing us with other creatures. He observed his family's dogs and cats and the horses in the lanes near his home, and he spent long hours at the Zoological Gardens in London, studying the faces of the monkeys. Animals, unlike people, cannot easily pretend to feel what they do not, which made them excellent and honest teachers for his purpose.

To discover whether people everywhere show their feelings in the same way, Darwin wrote a list of questions and sent it to friends, missionaries and other travellers living in distant parts of the world. Did a person there blush when ashamed, shake the head for no, or frown when puzzled? The answers came back by sea over many months, and he sorted them with the care of a man arranging a very large puzzle.

A face moves too quickly to be drawn from memory, and an artist's picture may easily show what the artist expects instead of what is really there. Darwin therefore filled his book with photographs, among them pictures by the London photographer Oscar Rejlander, which was then a bold and costly thing to do. The result was one of the first science books in which the evidence could be seen directly with the eyes.

A French doctor named Duchenne had touched small electric currents to the faces of volunteers, causing individual muscles to twitch while a camera recorded the result. Because no feeling was behind these faces, they showed with great clarity exactly which muscle produces which look. Darwin borrowed the photographs gratefully, though he knew that a face moved by wires could look strangely false.

The first of Darwin's three principles is that an action which once served a useful purpose may become a habit, and may then be repeated even when it serves no purpose at all. A pet dog circling on a soft rug before it lies down is copying, he thought, the movements of wild ancestors that trampled the grass to make a bed. The habit has long outlived its reason, yet the dog still obeys it as faithfully as ever.

Darwin noticed that a person struggling to recall a name will often lift the eyebrows and stare upward, as if the answer were written somewhere on the ceiling. Raising the brows opens the eyes wide, which is useful when we are trying to see something, and he suspected that the movement had become so linked with effort that it now accompanies even an effort of memory. We copy the old habit of looking hard, even though there is nothing in front of us to see.

Darwin's second principle, which he named antithesis, holds that opposite feelings tend to produce opposite movements, even when the movements have no direct use. A dog preparing to fight walks stiffly, with its head high, its ears pricked, the hair on its neck bristling and its tail held erect. Every part of the body seems to say that it is large, strong and ready.

When the same dog meets its master, every part of its body does exactly the reverse of what it did when it meant to fight. The back sinks low, the ears fall back, the fur lies smooth, and the tail swings from side to side as the whole animal wriggles with pleasure. Darwin thought the dog was not learning these movements anywhere, but simply doing the opposite of its angry self.

Cats, Darwin observed, follow the same law of opposites with their own special movements. An angry cat crouches low, flattens its ears and lashes its tail, while a cat that loves its owner rises on its legs, lifts its tail and rubs its head and flank against any friendly hand or leg. One of these cats looks ready to spring, the other ready to be stroked.

The third principle concerns the body's own machinery: when a feeling grows strong enough, the nervous system discharges its excitement in ways that no one has chosen and no one can easily stop. Hands shake, the skin sweats, the heart pounds and the voice trembles, whether or not any of it does the person the slightest good. Darwin did not pretend to understand every detail of how this works, and said so openly.

Fear, Darwin wrote, shakes the whole body at once: the heart gallops, the skin turns pale and damp, the muscles tremble and the mouth becomes so dry that the voice may crack or fail altogether. These signs are not performed for anyone's benefit, and the afraid person would often hide them gladly if the will had any power over them. In this honesty, he thought, lay the strongest proof that the body obeys rules older than thought.

In a frightened or furious animal the hair rises along the back and neck, which makes the creature look larger and fiercer than it really is. Humans, having lost most of their body hair, can no longer perform this trick, yet in moments of cold or terror the skin still pimples and the few hairs still lift. Darwin took this as a faint echo of an ancient habit, still in the body long after its purpose had gone.

The voice, Darwin pointed out, is as expressive as the face, for animals of many kinds growl, bark, purr or shriek according to their mood. High, sharp sounds suit alarm and pain, while low, steady ones suit anger and comfort, and he suspected that the voices of human beings had grown out of the same ancient family of calls. A child's scream and a puppy's yelp may not be so different, after all.

At the zoo, Darwin watched the keepers tickle young chimpanzees, and he noted that the animals produced a panting sound very like a human laugh, and that their eyes seemed to shine with fun. If an ape can laugh when tickled, he argued, then laughter cannot be a human invention, but must be an old inheritance that we share with our nearest relatives. Modern researchers have since found playful sounds of this kind in other animals too.

Darwin devoted close attention to the ears, because in horses and dogs they move so readily with the mood. An angry horse presses its ears flat against the neck, bares its teeth and prepares to bite, so that the ears seem to say in advance what the jaws intend to do. The flat ears also protect the animal, he supposed, when it fights, and so the habit may have started as both a warning and a safeguard.

When a person sneers, one corner of the lip lifts so that the tooth beneath it may show, usually on a single side of the face. Darwin believed that this small movement was a faint memory of the snarl of an ancestor ready to fight, now softened into a gesture of contempt or defiance. We do not mean to threaten when we sneer, he said, yet the shape of the old threat remains.

At the Zoological Gardens, Darwin saw a young chimpanzee that had been refused a piece of fruit push its lips far forward into a long pout, and he noted that a sulky human child does very much the same. Such resemblances between a chimpanzee and a child, he felt, were far too exact to be mere accidents of chance. They were the sort of quiet evidence, collected across many afternoons, on which his larger argument slowly came to rest.

A screaming baby squeezes the eyes shut, and the muscles round them tighten until the face is a mask of wrinkles. Darwin thought that this protects the eyes from the rush of blood that comes with hard screaming, but modern researchers are not convinced by that explanation, and the question is still open. What he saw, however, was exactly right, as any parent who has endured a sleepless night will gladly confirm.

Adults weep when they grieve, and Darwin suggested that the habit is a kind of inheritance from infancy, when the muscles of a screaming child squeeze the tear glands without any plan. As we grow, the screaming is controlled, but the gentle flow of tears remains. He admitted that it was hard to prove, since tears belong to the most private part of human life and are difficult to observe.

In sorrow and anxiety, Darwin observed, the inner ends of the eyebrows are drawn upward, and the corners of the mouth are pulled downward, so that the face seems to droop beneath some invisible weight. He found the same pattern in photographs, in paintings, in the faces of his own family and in the replies of his correspondents abroad. It was, he concluded, one of the most reliable and most widely understood of all human signals.

Darwin gave the name of grief muscles to the small bands above the eyes that produce the sad look, and he noticed that very few people can move them at will. Yet they move almost by themselves when a person is truly distressed, which makes the sad expression among the hardest for an actor to counterfeit. A real feeling, he remarked, writes in a handwriting that cannot easily be forged.

In deep despair, wrote Darwin, a person's whole body seems to lose its spring: the head sinks forward, the limbs hang loosely, the pulse slows and the movements become few and heavy. He took great care to describe such moments with sympathy and without drama, aware that they were the saddest chapters of any life. The body, in his account, simply stops spending energy it can no longer afford.

Joy, Darwin observed, is a feeling that seems to overflow the body and demand movement: children jump, clap their hands and dance, and a happy dog bounds across the grass in great, ridiculous circles. The face brightens, the eyes sparkle and the breathing quickens as the whole being goes lively. Pleasure, in his view, is not a quiet thing, but a sort of energy that has nowhere else to go.

During a hearty laugh the mouth opens, the corners of the lips lift, and the muscles around the eyes tighten until the lower lids are puckered into small folds. Darwin noted with pleasure that the laughter sometimes grows so strong that tears begin to flow, so that joy and sorrow share a curious likeness in the eye. It is one of the odd facts of the human face that these two feelings can look so alike.

Love and tenderness, Darwin observed, hardly show on the face at all, and are better read in what the body does: the soft smile, the lingering touch, the warm voice and the wish to hold. A mother with her baby needs no words, for her whole manner tells the child that it is safe. He admitted that such feelings were harder to describe than anger or fear, being so gentle.

When a person thinks hard or faces a difficulty, the eyebrows draw together and downward until a furrow appears between them. Darwin believed that this frown began as a way of shielding the eyes from glare, and that it later became attached to any effort of the mind, whether or not the sun was shining. We frown at a maths problem, he said, as our ancestors frowned at a bright sky.

A sulky child folds the arms, lowers the head, frowns and pushes the lips forward in a way that is understood at a glance by anyone who has ever dealt with children. Darwin noted that his correspondents described the same sulky look in the young of many peoples, as though it belonged to no particular country at all. Bad temper, it appeared, is spoken in a language that needs no translation, and that children everywhere seem to learn without lessons.

A person who has resolved to carry out a difficult task will often close the mouth tightly and set the jaw, as though sealing the decision inside. Darwin took this firm closing of the lips to be the natural sign of resolve, and he found it described in nearly every region from which he received replies. The face, in other words, announces to everyone nearby what the mind has already quietly decided.

Anger, Darwin recorded, sends the blood rushing to the face, quickens the heart and breathing, widens the nostrils, sets the teeth together and draws the fists tight, as though the whole body were preparing to strike. He found the same preparation in animals that are about to fight, and he thought it plain that the human face still carries the posture of battle. A man may stay calm in his words, yet his face often tells the story of a struggle.

In strong hatred and rage, Darwin wrote, the eyes glare fixedly, the lips draw back, the head and chest lean toward the enemy and the whole posture grows threatening. Even a person who is trying with all their will to remain calm may betray the feeling through some tiny movement of the face, such as a tightening of the lip. The body, he said, remembers how to fight long after the mind has promised to keep the peace.

A person who feels contempt or scorn is apt to turn the face aside, to raise the nose a little and to give a short snort, as though something unpleasant were in the air. Darwin saw in this the symbolic act of getting rid of a bad smell, a movement that has now been transferred from objects to people and ideas. We express our disapproval, he wrote, by performing the old act of refusal, long after the bad smell has gone.

Disgust, Darwin argued, began with the rejection of bad food: the nose wrinkles, the lips are pushed out or twisted, and the tongue may even be thrust forward to spit. The expression is seen in very young infants, which suggests that it is not learned from other people, though the things that disgust us later in life are certainly shaped by custom. The movement of the face and the habit of refusal were, in his view, born together.

Someone who feels guilty will usually let the eyes wander, refusing to meet the gaze of the person who knows the truth, and Darwin observed that the head droops as though weighed down. Pride works in exactly the opposite way, lifting the head and chest and drawing the eyes upward, in another example of his law of opposites. The eyes, he observed, can seldom keep a secret from other eyes, and the guilty person seems to know it well.

The shrug, said Darwin, is the body's way of saying that one cannot, or does not know, or does not care to try, and it combines raised shoulders, elbows pressed to the sides, open palms and lifted brows. His correspondents reported the gesture from several quarters of the world, and he thought it a good example of a habit that is shared and not taught. It says a great deal without a single word, and it is understood almost at once by anyone watching.

Darwin asked whether the nod of agreement and the shake of refusal belong to all of humankind, and the answers he received suggested that they are common but not universal. A baby turning the head from the spoon, he suggested, may be the origin of the shake, and the nod may be its opposite, though he was careful to call this a guess. Not every habit of the body, he concluded, is simply inherited, since some gestures are certainly taught by custom and example.

In surprise the eyebrows lift high, the eyes open wide, and the mouth falls slightly open, so that for a moment the face is empty of everything but attention. Darwin reasoned that the raised brows and wide eyes are the natural way of taking in as much of a new sight as possible, as quickly as possible. A moment later, he added, the surprise turns into either delight or alarm, depending on what the new sight turns out to be.

Fear, in Darwin's description, opens the eyes wide, drains the colour from the cheeks, makes the hair stand on end and sets the heart racing, so that the whole person is ready either to freeze or to flee. In extreme terror, he said, the heart may seem to stop for an instant and the voice may fail entirely. The old fight-or-flight response lies beneath every cold shiver, though Darwin did not use those words.

At the Zoological Gardens, Darwin pressed his face to the thick glass of a puff adder's cage and resolved, with all his determination, not to flinch when the snake struck at him. He knew perfectly well that the glass would protect him, and that he was in no danger of any kind. The snake, however, had its own opinion of the matter, and it was about to express it.

When the snake finally struck against the glass, Darwin leapt backwards a yard or more, in complete defiance of his own will and reason, and he reported the fact with some amusement. The little experiment showed him that the body's alarm acts before the thinking mind can argue with it. Some reactions, he concluded, are far older and far faster than any decision of ours.

In terror and horror, wrote Darwin, a person may cry out, shake from head to foot, break into a cold sweat and try to run, or else stand frozen to the spot with staring eyes. The body prepares for a danger that the mind has barely begun to recognise. He placed these violent signs at the far end of the scale from mild surprise, and linked them by gradual steps.

Shyness and shame, Darwin noted, make a person lower the eyes, turn the head aside, and sometimes try to hide the face altogether, as if to avoid being seen. He thought that these feelings arise from a keen awareness of other people's opinions, and from attention directed inward to ourselves. The shy person is, in a sense, too busy thinking about his own appearance.

Blushing, Darwin declared, is the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions, for no animal, so far as he could find out, reddens in the face from shame. He listed the many ways in which people blush, and noted that the reaction cannot be summoned by the will, for the command to blush only makes the cheeks burn the more. Few things in his book gave him such delight as this flush of colour.

The cause of blushing, he believed, lies in our attention to what other people think of us, and especially of our appearance, which sends the blood flowing to the cheeks and often the neck. Scientists today still argue about the exact reasons, and some of Darwin's explanations have not survived later research. Yet his central observation, that blushing is a social blush and not merely a physical one, remains widely accepted.

As the answers arrived from Australia, India, Africa, North America and elsewhere, Darwin saw that people of very different customs often described the very same expressions on the face. Laughter, sulking, blushing and astonishment appeared, with small differences, in all parts of the world. He read this as strong evidence that all human beings, whatever their customs, share one common inheritance.

Darwin concluded that the main expressions are not inventions of culture, but part of the inheritance of the body, and that they join us to the animals from which we are descended. The conclusion fitted his larger theory, and added a new kind of evidence to it, drawn from living faces instead of old bones. It also reminded his readers that humans, for all their pride, share their feelings with a wide family.

A century and a half later, scientists are still arguing over Darwin's claims, and the debate has not ended. Some experiments suggest that a few basic expressions are recognised in almost every culture, while others show that the way we read a face depends heavily on where and how we grew up. Darwin himself, who valued honest doubt, would probably have been delighted to see the question still alive.

Darwin closed his book by reminding readers that the study of expression teaches us how closely human beings are bound to one another, and to the animals that came before us. A face, he suggested, is a window through which an honest feeling can be seen, and it is a language that nearly everyone, from the youngest infant to the oldest sailor, can read at least in part. That, in the end, is why his book is still worth reading, and still alive.
